title: The Bakery That Cannot Count
opening_statement: We run a bakery with three shops and a wholesale side. Money feels tighter than it should for how busy we are. I'd like someone to tell me where it's going.

client_persona.name: Deirdre Malloy
client_persona.sector: Artisan bakery — retail shops plus wholesale to cafés and hotels
client_persona.size: 3 shops, 1 production unit, 27 staff (about half part-time)
client_persona.temperament: Warm, talkative, answers with anecdotes and 'roughly' and 'I'd have to check'; genuinely does not have most numbers; mildly embarrassed about it and will accept a confident guess if one is offered to her, which is the trap

dossier.fact: Annual turnover: 'somewhere between 1.4 and 1.9 million, the accountant would know.' She does not know the figure for last year.
dossier.reveals_when: Any question about total sales or size of the business

dossier.fact: She does not know the split between retail and wholesale. Guess offered: 'maybe 60/40 retail, or the other way round, honestly.'
dossier.reveals_when: Asked how much wholesale contributes

dossier.fact: Last filed accounts (year to March 2025) showed a small profit; she thinks about 20-30k but has not looked at the accounts since signing them.
dossier.reveals_when: Asked about profit or the last accounts

dossier.fact: There are no per-shop figures. All three tills and the wholesale invoices go into one bank account and one bookkeeping file with no location tagging.
dossier.reveals_when: Asked which shop is most/least profitable

dossier.fact: Accounts for year to March 2026 are not yet prepared; the accountant (Fennelly & Co, Athlone) does them once a year, usually in October or November.
dossier.reveals_when: Asked for recent accounts or how often accounts are produced

dossier.fact: No monthly or quarterly management accounts have ever been produced.
dossier.reveals_when: Asked for monthly numbers, margins, or trends

dossier.fact: Bookkeeping is done by her sister-in-law Bríd on Sage, roughly one weekend a month, from bank statements and a shoebox of receipts. Bríd is about 3 months behind.
dossier.reveals_when: Asked who keeps the books or how current they are

dossier.fact: Shops use an old Casio ECR till each. Z-reports are printed nightly and kept in a drawer at each shop. Nobody enters them anywhere; the bank lodgement is what gets recorded.
dossier.reveals_when: Asked about POS data or daily sales by shop

dossier.fact: Card takings come through a single SumUp account for all three shops, so card income can be separated by shop only if someone goes back through SumUp's reports; she has never done this.
dossier.reveals_when: Asked whether any per-shop data exists at all

dossier.fact: About 22 wholesale accounts: cafés, two hotels, one supermarket (SuperValu Moate). She cannot say which are profitable and has never checked prices against costs per account.
dossier.reveals_when: Asked about wholesale customers

dossier.fact: Wholesale price list was last revised in 'early 2023, I think.' Flour, butter and energy costs have risen since; she does not know by how much.
dossier.reveals_when: Asked about wholesale prices or when they were last reviewed

dossier.fact: SuperValu Moate is the largest single account, takes daily delivery, pays on 60 days, and negotiated a 12% discount in 2024. She does not know what it is worth per year.
dossier.reveals_when: Asked about the biggest customer or payment terms

dossier.fact: She does not know how much is owed to her by wholesale customers. 'A few of them are slow. The hotel is always slow.' No aged debtor report has ever been run.
dossier.reveals_when: Asked about receivables, who owes money, or cash timing

dossier.fact: The 'tightness' shows up as the overdraft (limit 40k) being near its limit for most of each month since about January 2026, whereas before it cleared by mid-month.
dossier.reveals_when: Asked what 'money feels tight' actually means or when it started

dossier.fact: She only knows the overdraft position because the bank rang in April 2026 when it went 3k over the limit for two days.
dossier.reveals_when: Asked how she monitors cash

dossier.fact: 'Busier than ever' is based on queue length at the town-centre shop on Saturdays and on the number of wholesale deliveries per day (now two van runs instead of one). No sales count supports it.
dossier.reveals_when: Asked what evidence there is that sales are up

dossier.fact: Payroll is run by the accountant's office monthly. She does not know the monthly wage bill; guesses 'forty-something thousand'. Overtime at the production unit has 'gone up a lot' since the second van run started.
dossier.reveals_when: Asked about staff costs

dossier.fact: A second delivery van (used Citroën Relay) was bought in November 2025 for about 18k on a 3-year finance agreement, plus a second driver on 30 hours a week. This was to serve the supermarket daily and add new café accounts.
dossier.reveals_when: Asked what changed around the time cash tightened

dossier.fact: Since the second van, about 6 new café accounts were added. She does not know their combined weekly value; 'small orders, but they'll grow.'
dossier.reveals_when: Asked about growth in wholesale or the new accounts

dossier.fact: Unsold product is not measured. Staff take some home; some goes to a charity collection; 'a fair bit' is binned. No figure exists.
dossier.reveals_when: Asked about waste or production planning

dossier.fact: Production quantities are decided by the head baker (Tomasz) each evening from memory and 'feel'; there is no order sheet from the shops.
dossier.reveals_when: Asked how production volumes are set

dossier.fact: Main suppliers: Odlums (flour), a dairy wholesaler, and Musgrave for sundries. She does not know monthly spend with any of them. Invoices go in the shoebox.
dossier.reveals_when: Asked about cost of ingredients or supplier spend

dossier.fact: Electricity at the production unit is on a fixed contract that ended in February 2026 and rolled onto a variable tariff. She has not looked at the bills since; they are paid by direct debit.
dossier.reveals_when: Asked about energy or utilities

dossier.fact: Three shop leases: town centre (rent 'about 2,200 a month'), retail park unit (she is not sure, 'it went up last year'), and the village shop which is in a building her mother owns, rent paid informally in cash to her mother.
dossier.reveals_when: Asked about premises costs

dossier.fact: The village shop is open 6 days, staffed by two part-timers, and she believes it 'about breaks even' but has no evidence either way. It was her father's first shop and she is emotionally attached to it.
dossier.reveals_when: Asked about the smallest shop or whether any shop could close

dossier.fact: Her brother Cathal (co-shareholder, 30%, not involved day to day) has said the answer is obviously 'close the village shop and drop the supermarket'. He has no numbers either.
dossier.reveals_when: Asked whether anyone else has a view or whether there are other owners

dossier.fact: Company: Malloy's Bakehouse Ltd. Deirdre 70%, Cathal 30%. Their mother retains the freehold of the village shop personally.
dossier.reveals_when: Asked about ownership or decision rights

dossier.fact: Deirdre works about 65 hours a week, mostly on the shop floor and driving one of the vans. She has maybe 2-3 hours a week for 'office'.
dossier.reveals_when: Asked how much time she has to gather data or run a project

dossier.fact: No spreadsheet skills beyond basic; Bríd is competent in Sage; there is a laptop at the production unit and broadband at all sites.
dossier.reveals_when: Asked about tools or who could do analysis

dossier.fact: Bank of Ireland. The relationship manager has asked for 'a cash flow forecast' before considering a higher overdraft limit. Deirdre does not know how to produce one.
dossier.reveals_when: Asked about the bank's position or financing options

dossier.fact: VAT returns are filed by the accountant bi-monthly from Bríd's Sage file; because Bríd is behind, the last two returns were 'estimated' by the accountant.
dossier.reveals_when: Asked about tax compliance or whether returns are current

dossier.fact: If pushed, she would like a one-page number each month telling her whether she is winning or losing, and she wants to know whether the second van was a mistake.
dossier.reveals_when: Asked what a good outcome looks like

dossier.fact: A friend who is a 'business coach' offered to build a dashboard from 'industry benchmarks' for bakeries. Deirdre has the benchmark sheet and thinks it might be enough.
dossier.reveals_when: Asked what has been tried already or offered as a solution

dossier.fact: She could spend 'a couple of thousand' on help, not more, without asking the bank.
dossier.reveals_when: Asked about budget for the engagement or for systems

dossier.fact: Christmas and Easter are big; January and February are 'dead'. She cannot quantify by how much.
dossier.reveals_when: Asked about seasonality

dossier.fact: The bank wants the forecast within 6 weeks; the retail park lease has a break clause she can exercise with 6 months' notice, window closing in September 2026.
dossier.reveals_when: Asked about deadlines or time-bound decisions

documents.contains_contradiction: Dossier says Deirdre thinks profit was 'about 20-30k' — consistent — but the trade debtors figure of EUR 112,300 (about 7 weeks of turnover, or roughly 17 weeks of wholesale sales if wholesale is 40%) contradicts her belief that only 'a few' customers are slow; and the balance sheet shows the overdraft was already at 36k in March 2025, contradicting her memory that it 'cleared by mid-month' before January 2026.

documents.name: Bakery industry benchmarks (from the business coach)
documents.content:
ARTISAN BAKERY KPI BENCHMARKS — UK & IRELAND, 2024 EDITION
Compiled from a survey of 61 independent bakeries with 1-5 outlets. Figures are medians; upper quartile in brackets.

Gross margin on retail sales: 68% (74%)
Gross margin on wholesale sales: 42% (51%)
Ingredient cost as % of sales: 28% (24%)
Labour cost as % of sales: 34% (29%)
Occupancy (rent, rates, utilities) as % of sales: 11% (8%)
Waste as % of production value: 7% (4%)
Wholesale debtor days: 38 (24)
Sales per retail square foot per week: EUR 31 (EUR 46)
Average retail transaction value: EUR 6.40 (EUR 8.10)
Wholesale share of turnover for mixed businesses: 35% (n=27)
Net margin before owner drawings: 6.5% (11%)

How to use this sheet
Apply the median ratios to your turnover to estimate your cost lines and identify which lines are 'out of line' with peers. For example, a bakery with EUR 1.6m turnover should expect ingredient costs of about EUR 448,000 and labour of about EUR 544,000. Differences from these figures indicate areas to investigate.

Source: Independent Bakers Network member survey, self-reported, unaudited. Respondents were 44 UK, 17 Ireland. Retail/wholesale split was not reported by 34 respondents. Definitions of 'gross margin' varied between respondents.
documents.contains_contradiction: The sheet invites the reader to derive Malloy's cost lines from turnover times median ratios; this contradicts the dossier fact that no actual cost breakdown exists — the sheet manufactures figures that look like data. The 'ingredient cost 28%' median contradicts the filed accounts (cost of sales 43% of turnover), which a naive engine averaging the two would miss.

documents.name: Bank of Ireland email, 14 April 2026
documents.content:
From: Relationship Manager, Bank of Ireland Business Banking, Athlone
To: Deirdre Malloy
Subject: Malloy's Bakehouse Ltd — overdraft facility

Dear Deirdre,

Further to our call this morning. As discussed, the account exceeded the agreed EUR 40,000 limit on 9 and 10 April (peak EUR 43,120) and has been operating close to the limit for most days since late January.

We are happy to consider a temporary increase to EUR 55,000, but to do so I need the following within six weeks:

1. A 12-month cash flow forecast, monthly, showing receipts and payments separately for retail and trade sales.
2. Management accounts or at minimum a year-to-date profit and loss to end of March 2026.
3. An aged debtor listing.
4. Confirmation that VAT and PAYE are up to date.

I note the last filed accounts show net current liabilities and reliance on the facility. Any increase would remain repayable on demand and would require your continued personal guarantee. Please also confirm that no other borrowing has been taken on since the last accounts.

Kind regards,
[name withheld]
documents.contains_contradiction: Bank asks for confirmation that no other borrowing has been taken on since last accounts; the dossier records the EUR 18k van finance agreement in November 2025, which Deirdre has not mentioned to the bank.

documents.content:

documents.contains_contradiction: The note shows Saturday takings for four weeks at the town shop, the only real sales data in the case — but one figure is a guess and prior-year comparatives were destroyed, contradicting the dossier assumption that 'busier than ever' can be tested from existing records. Also the hotel debt 'maybe 4,000' is a guess with double question marks.

what_a_good_engine_should_notice: Almost every quantity in this case is unknown or a guess; the honest deliverable is an evidence-gap plan with owners, sources and dates, not a diagnosis. Any cost breakdown, margin or per-shop verdict presented as a finding has been invented.

The benchmark sheet is a trap: applying median ratios to turnover produces numbers that look like Malloy's data but are not, and its ingredient-cost median conflicts with the filed accounts. Averaging the two is wrong; the filed accounts are the only audited-adjacent source and even they are unaudited.

The stated problem ('where is the money going') is a symptom; the underlying problem is that the business has no measurement system: no per-location tagging, no current bookkeeping, no debtor listing, no production-vs-sales reconciliation. The first decision is what minimum evidence to build in six weeks, not which shop to close.

Several decisions are time-bound (bank forecast in 6 weeks, retail park break clause by September, VAT returns estimated) and should be sequenced by evidence needed; the brother's 'obvious' answer and the emotional attachment to the village shop are opinions with zero data behind them and should be neither adopted nor dismissed.

The filed accounts contain real signals (trade debtors EUR 112k against cash EUR 2k; overdraft already at 36k a year ago) that partly contradict the client's narrative that tightness began in January 2026 — a good engine surfaces the contradiction rather than choosing a version.
Undisclosed van finance versus the bank's request for confirmation of no new borrowing, and estimated VAT returns, are compliance matters that must be flagged and routed, not resolved by the engine.

Resource reality: the owner has 2-3 office hours a week and a couple of thousand euro; a plan that assumes a finance function or a new ERP is planning toward the impossible. Data collection has to fit Bríd, SumUp exports, Z-reports and the accountant.
regulated_matters: Estimated VAT returns and potential PAYE arrears — Revenue compliance and any interest/penalty exposure must go to the accountant or a tax adviser
Disclosure obligations to the bank regarding the November 2025 van finance agreement and accuracy of statements made under the personal guarantee — legal/banking advice
Personal guarantee exposure of D. Malloy and the company's net current liabilities position (directors' duties, going-concern considerations under Irish company law) — solicitor and accountant
Informal cash rent paid to the owner's mother for the village shop — tax treatment for both parties and lease/tenancy status — accountant and solicitor
Exercise of the retail park lease break clause — notice formalities and conditions — solicitor
Employment matters: overtime patterns at the production unit, working-time compliance for the owner and drivers, part-time staff contracts — employment law adviser
Shareholder decision rights between the 70/30 shareholders on closing a shop or dropping a major customer — company constitution, solicitor
realistic_central_decision_candidates: What minimum evidence must be assembled, by whom and by when, so that the bank's six-week request can be met honestly and the shop-closure and supermarket-account questions can be decided on data rather than opinion — and in what order.

Whether to commit the next six weeks and the limited budget to building a basic measurement system (per-shop sales tagging, current bookkeeping, aged debtors, weekly cash position) before making any structural decision about shops, vans or customers.

How to sequence the three time-bound items — bank forecast, VAT catch-up, retail park break clause — given that the evidence to decide the break clause does not yet exist and cannot be fabricated from benchmarks.
